paragraphs: §1 — Jeroboam son of Nebat, the first to introduce schism

The first to bring forth dissension in the religion, to sow transgressions among the House of Israel after the kingship was firmly established, and to alter the religious duties and exchange them, was Jeroboam — for Scripture says of him in more than one place [1 Kgs 14:16; 15:30, and elsewhere]: "אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וַאֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל." This was in his fashioning of the "[calves of] gold," and in his saying to the nation [1 Kgs 12:28]: "רַב לָכֶם מֵעֲלוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם."

What drove him to this — as Scripture reports — was his seeking to secure the kingship and keep it for himself, and his fear that the people, on going up to Jerusalem, would be drawn to their [rightful] king, who was of the seed of David, so that the kingship would slip from his hand. For Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:26–28]: "וַיֹּאמֶר יָרָבְעָם בְּלִבּוֹ: עַתָּה תָּשׁוּב הַמַּמְלָכָה לְבֵית דָּוִד. אִם יַעֲלֶה הָעָם הַזֶּה לַעֲשׂוֹת זְבָחִים בְּבֵית ה' בִּירוּשָׁלִַם, וְשָׁב לֵב הָעָם הַזֶּה אֶל אֲדֹנֵיהֶם אֶל רְחַבְעָם מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה וַהֲרָגֻנִי, וְשָׁבוּ אֶל רְחַבְעָם מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה. וַיִּוָּעַץ הַמֶּלֶךְ וַיַּעַשׂ שְׁנֵי עֶגְלֵי זָהָב וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם: רַב לָכֶם מֵעֲלוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם, הִנֵּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלוּךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם."

A group of our companions has held that he took these two calves only to set them up in the place of the "Cherubim," and this view is not far-fetched — for everything he adopted and dissented in, he meant only as an imitation and a counterfeit of what had been prescribed. The proof of this is his replacing the priests with men from the rest of the nation, for Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:31]: "וַיַּעַשׂ כֹּהֲנִים מִקְצוֹת הָעָם אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָיוּ מִבְּנֵי לֵוִי"; and likewise his appointing the festival in the eighth month in place of the seventh, in the manner of the festival kept in the Temple, for Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:32]: "וַיַּעַשׂ יָרָבְעָם חָג בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁמִינִי בַּחֲמִשָּׁה־עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ כֶּחָג אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה." It may be that he gave the people to suppose that the year was intercalated, as a group of our companions has said.
§2 — That Jeroboam was no idolater

This, then, is what Scripture reports that Jeroboam dissented in and exchanged. It may well be that he dissented in many other duties besides, altering and exchanging them, only that Scripture did not mention them, but confined itself to citing the gravest and greatest. For Jeroboam was not one who disbelieved in the Creator — exalted be His mention — nor who denied Him, nor who worshipped an idol, as some imagine.

We know this from two directions. The first is what we have already noted: his replacing every duty with another in its place. Had he gone outside the religion altogether, he would have dropped the duty entirely, abolished it, and done away with it, having no need to substitute for it; rather, the cause of his substituting and altering was, as we said, his dread of losing the kingship. The second direction by which we know he had not departed from the religion nor worshipped an idol is this: we see that Jehu utterly destroyed the idols and slew their worshippers in Israel — for Scripture says of him [2 Kgs 10:28]: "וַיַּשְׁמֵד יֵהוּא אֶת הַבַּעַל מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל" — and we then see it reported that he persisted in the sins of Jeroboam, as it says [ibid. 10:29]: "רַק חַטָּאֵי יָרָבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא סָר יֵהוּא מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם, עֶגְלֵי הַזָּהָב אֲשֶׁר בֵּית אֵל וַאֲשֶׁר בְּדָן." This is among the clearest proofs that his taking of the calves was not for him as the idolaters' idols are for them.

Should someone object: "Has not Scripture reported that he sacrificed to them and offered incense, for it says [1 Kgs 12:32] 'לְזַבֵּחַ לָעֲגָלִים אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה,' and says in another place 'לְהַקְטִיר לָעֲגָלִים אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה'?" — we answer: it is Scripture's way to employ such [language]. Namely, anyone who adopts something hateful to God, in which there is dissent from the religion, Scripture ascribes to him that he has "worshipped it" and "taken it [as a god]." This is like His saying [Deut 4:28]: "וַעֲבַדְתֶּם שָׁם אֱלֹהִים מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי אָדָם עֵץ וָאֶבֶן אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִרְאוּן וְלֹא יִשְׁמְעוּן וְלֹא יֹאכְלוּן וְלֹא יְרִיחֻן" — yet the Children of Israel did not worship an idol in the Exile; rather, [Scripture] meant the transgressions that idolaters commit. So too His saying [Lev 18:3]: "כְּמַעֲשֵׂה אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם אֲשֶׁר יְשַׁבְתֶּם בָּהּ לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ, וּכְמַעֲשֵׂה אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי מֵבִיא אֶתְכֶם שָׁמָּה לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ, וּבְחֻקֹּתֵיהֶם לֹא תֵלֵכוּ" — for He then made clear that He meant in this place the forbidden unions.

Scripture likewise ascribes to one who pours out his desire upon a particular thing, prefers it, and prizes it, that "he sacrifices to it and offers it incense." This is like His saying [Hab 1:16]: "עַל כֵּן יְזַבֵּחַ לְחֶרְמוֹ וִיקַטֵּר לְמִכְמַרְתּוֹ, כִּי בָהֵמָּה שָׁמֵן חֶלְקוֹ וּמַאֲכָלוֹ בְּרִאָה." For it is absurd that a man should sacrifice and burn incense to the net and the snare with which he hunts; rather, [Scripture] meant the inclining of his heart toward them, that they are the cause of his ease and that by them he made his living broad. So too Jeroboam offered incense in the House of God — exalted be His praise — and set [the calves] over against the Cherubim, and so was said to "sacrifice and offer incense" [to them]; for the Creator had forbidden the taking of [such] images and the offering and incense save in the chosen place. One who dissents in this, taking an image and sacrificing and offering by it and over against it, is as though he had already offered to it.

And since the Creator — exalted and sanctified — calls one who sacrificed outside the camp "one who sacrificed to other than God" — as He says [Lev 17:7]: "וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד אֶת זִבְחֵיהֶם לַשְּׂעִירִם אֲשֶׁר הֵם זֹנִים אַחֲרֵיהֶם" — we know once more that one who sacrificed and offered incense beside an image deserves to have it said of him that he "sacrificed and offered incense to it."
§3 — "These are your gods, O Israel"

As for His saying "הִנֵּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל," it may be that he meant by it to point toward the Creator and toward the place at which one offers to Him, intending [thereby] the goal of prayer and offering at it. This is like the Children of Israel's saying to Aaron [Exod 32:1]: "קוּם עֲשֵׂה לָנוּ אֱלֹהִים," and their saying when the calf appeared [ibid. 32:4]: "אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל." Did they not say to him, "עֲשֵׂה לָנוּ אֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ לְפָנֵינוּ"? Yet the departure from Egypt had already passed, and the thing they were asking to be made did not yet exist! How could a thing not-yet-existing accomplish what had already happened and gone by? Could such a statement come from anyone not deprived of his reason?

What ought to be said in this connection is that the form of the calf is the likeness of one of the faces of the angels, as He says [Ezek 1:10]: "וּפְנֵי שׁוֹר מֵהַשְּׂמֹאול." The Children of Israel, in saying of the calf "אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל," meant: this is the form of the angel that brought us out of Egypt — for Scripture says [Exod 14:19]: "וַיִּסַּע מַלְאַךְ הָאֱלֹהִים הַהֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵי מַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל." And it may be that Jeroboam meant the same.
§4 — The root of Israel's schism

From that hour — I mean the hour in which Jeroboam did what he did — dissension welled up among the Children of Israel and those doctrines were sown among them, and they and their successors inherited them one from another. For [Scripture] says of each one of their kings, "וַיֵּלֶךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ יָרָבְעָם וּבְחַטָּאתוֹ אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל." Nor did they cease from this until the Ten Tribes were exiled. For [Scripture] says, concerning Shalmaneser when he exiled Hoshea son of Elah in the days of Hezekiah and exiled the rest of the tribes [2 Kgs 17:22]: "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לֹא סָרוּ מִמֶּנָּה." So at the very moment of their being carried into exile they stood upon the sins of Jeroboam — that is, upon the doctrines and the lax rulings that he innovated, exchanged, and dissented in. By now the two calves had already been done away with: for one of them Sennacherib had carried off, as it says [Hos 8:6] "כִּי שְׁבָבִים יִהְיֶה עֵגֶל שֹׁמְרוֹן," and [Hos 10:6] "גַּם אוֹתוֹ לְאַשּׁוּר יוּבָל מִנְחָה לְמֶלֶךְ יָרֵב." So we know that what is said of the Children of Israel at the time of the exile, "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם," refers to the doctrines and lax rulings that he innovated and invented and made into a substitute for the true duties.

Thereafter the Children of Judah, too, followed them in that dissension, as it says [2 Kgs 17:19]: "וְגַם יְהוּדָה לֹא שָׁמַר אֶת מִצְוֹת ה' אֱלֹהֵיהֶם," and it says, "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּחֻקּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ." They were all exiled while upon those doctrines, were scattered through the world, and have remained upon them, inheriting them down to this day.

Now perhaps some who read this chapter will object to its length, since my aim in this bab is only to name the sects, without mentioning the cause of their dissension. Let whoever this befalls know that I did so for a reason that will not escape one who has prolonged his thought upon the matter.
§5 — The Samaritans (the Cuthites)

After Jeroboam there arose the Samaritans. They are those whom the nation calls "the Cuthites," of whom Scripture says [2 Kgs 17:24]: "וַיָּבֵא מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר מִבָּבֶל וּמִכּוּתָה…." They are those of whom it is said [Ezra 4:1]: "צָרֵי יְהוּדָה וּבִנְיָמִן" — for [Scripture] reports of them that they approached the heads of the Children of Israel at the time they were building the Second Temple, saying [ibid. 4:2]: "וַיִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל זְרֻבָּבֶל וְאֶל רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת וַיֹּאמְרוּ לָהֶם: נִבְנֶה עִמָּכֶם," and "וְלוֹ אֲנַחְנוּ זֹבְחִים מִימֵי אֵסַר חַדֹּן מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר." It is reported of them that to this day they make mention of "Sanballat the Horonite," who was a chief among them.
§6 — The Rabbanites: Simeon the Just and the Great Assembly

After the Samaritans there appeared the heads of this sect — namely the Rabbanites. This was in the time of the Second Temple. The first of them mentioned is "Simeon," whom they call "Simeon the Just." They claim that he was of the remnant of the "Men of the Great Assembly," who, by their claim, were in the age of Ezra and Nehemiah. The heads of the Rabbanites are only [a succession within] a single group, since they followed those doctrines and lax rulings inherited from Jeroboam; for it was they who fixed them, fortified them, argued for them, and wrote down upon them the "Mishnah" and the rest.

Among them, one after another, there was at times one who may have brought out the truth in some one duty, yet they united against him and set themselves to oppose him. Such was "Gamaliel," who took the festival according to the sighting of the new moon, and such was "Eliezer son of Hyrcanus," who dissented from them concerning a [matter of] impurity in which they did not [rightly] judge the vessels impure: they decreed against him and separated from him, despite the standing of the wondrous signs attesting the truth of his statement and God's own testimony to it in their account. God forbid that this be in our view as they stated it — rather, they are the ones who report it. We shall later recount the substance of that story as they have told it among the Jews.
§7 — The Sadducees and the Boethusians

After the appearance of the Rabbanites there appeared the Sadducees, whose [founders] were "Zadok" and "Boethus." They were, according to what the Rabbanites have reported, the disciples of "Antigonus," who came after "Simeon the Just," and from "Simeon" they took. "Zadok" is the first who openly opposed the Rabbanites, appeared against them in dissent, and grasped somewhat of the truth. He wrote a book consisting mostly of disparagement of the Rabbanites and invective against them — except that he established nothing of what he said by proof, but stated it by way of mere assertion. Save in one matter: the prohibition of [marrying] the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, which he upheld by analogy (qiyās) to the paternal aunt and the daughter-in-law. As for "Boethus," he used to say that the Festival of Weeks falls only on the first day [of the week], as the ʿAnanites and a group of the Karaites say.
§8 — The Maghāriyya (the Cave Sect)

Thereafter appeared the sect called the "Maghāriyya." They were so named because their books were found in caves. Among them is the "Alexandrian," whose book is famous and well known, the greatest of the books of the Maghāriyya; and after it a small book called Sefer Yadūʿa (?), "a well-known, recognized book," which is likewise a good book. As for the rest of the books of the Maghāriyya, there is in them no book of [real] worth; most of them are tales resembling idle fables.
§9 — Jesus

Thereafter appeared "Jesus," of whom the Rabbanites say that he is "son of Pandera." He is the one known [in Arabic] as ʿĪsā ibn Maryam ("Jesus son of Mary"), and he was in the days of "Joshua son of Peraḥyah." It is said that "Joshua" was the maternal uncle of "Jesus." This was in the age of the Caesar, king of Rome, and in the time of the Second Temple; and the Rabbanites plotted against him until they killed him and crucified him.
§10 — The Qurʿiyya

It is said that on the Nile of Egypt, some twenty parasangs from al-Fusṭāṭ, there is a people called the "Qurʿiyya." They were so named because they use vessels of gourd (al-qarʿ) alone, to the exclusion of all else. Some of the reporters relate of them that they claim to be the descendants of "Yoḥanan son of Qareaḥ."
§11 — Bayt Hillel and Bayt Shammai

Thereafter the Rabbanites split into two sects: "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai." The people of Iraq settled upon the doctrine of "Bayt Hillel," and the people of al-Shām settled upon the doctrine of "Bayt Shammai." "Hillel" and "Shammai" took from "Shemaiah" and "Avtalyon." The dispute of "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai" was in three [matters], and one party killed a number of the other.
§12 — ʿObadiah / Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (the ʿĪsawiyya)

After those whom we have mentioned there appeared "ʿObadiah," known as Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī — [Iṣfahān being a city in Persia] — who laid claim to prophethood for himself. His appearance was in the days of "ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān." It is said that he sought to rebel against the ruling power; men followed him, an army gathered to him, he fought, and was killed. Some of his adherents claim that he was not killed, but that he entered a cleft in the mountain and nothing more was known of him. His [alleged] miracle, by the claim of his adherents, is that he was a tailor and was — as they claimed — an illiterate who could neither write nor read, yet he produced books and scrolls though no one had taught him. In Damascus there is a group of his adherents, known as the "ʿĪsawiyya."
§13 — Yudghan the Shepherd (the Yudghanites)

After "Abū ʿĪsā" there was "Yudghan," whom his adherents call "Raʿyā" — that is, the shepherd of the nation. It is said that he was the disciple of "Abū ʿĪsā ʿObadiah," and he too laid claim to prophethood for himself; his adherents claim that he is the Messiah.
§14 — ʿAnan the Exilarch

After "Yudghan" there was "ʿAnan the Exilarch (Raʾs al-Jālūt)," and this was in the days of "Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr." He is the first to set forth a great body of the truth concerning the religious duties; he was versed in the statements of the Rabbanites, and there was none among them who could fault his knowledge. It is reported of "Hai, head of the academy" that he and his father used to translate ʿAnan's book from Aramaic into Hebrew, and that nothing of his statements passed before them but that they recognized a root for it in the statements of the Rabbanites — except what he said concerning the firstborn, and concerning the distinction between [a child] conceived by a Jew and one conceived by the gentiles; they did not know whence he took this until they found it in the "Ḥazzānūt of Yannai." The Rabbanites strove to kill him, but could not reach him.
§15 — Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī

After "ʿAnan" there was "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī," and this was in the days of "al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh." Most of Ismaʿīl's words come down to ignorance, and whoever heard him among the people of solid knowledge would mock him; yet, for all his ignorance, he was inflamed with self-conceit, belittling "ʿAnan" in his books and deriding him much. It is reported of him that he told his adherents, when death came to him, to write upon his grave [2 Kgs 2:12]: "רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו."
§16 — Benjamin al-Nahāwandī

In the days of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" there was also "Benjamin al-Nahāwandī," who was likewise versed in the statements of the Rabbanites and strong in Scripture. It is said that he was God-fearing for many years, and that he succeeded in bringing out much of the truth. Yet in some places he would not make use of analogy (al-qiyās), but kept far from it; and his words indicate that he was bent on following the explicit text (al-naṣṣ), on derivation from the explicit text, or on what issues from analogy with two premises and a conclusion — which is the mean between analogy and the explicit text. We shall treat this chapter further in the Second Maqala.
§17 — Mūsā al-Zaʿfarānī / Abū ʿImrān al-Tiflīsī

Together with them and after them was "Mūsā al-Zaʿfarānī," known as "Abū ʿImrān al-Tiflīsī," who was of the people of Baghdad. He was called "al-Tiflīsī" only because he removed to Tiflīs — a city among the cities of Armenia — and settled there; a group followed his doctrine, and they remain there to this day. The adherents of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" claim that "Abū ʿImrān" was Ismaʿīl's disciple and took from him.
§18 — Mālik al-Ramlī
After them there was "Mālik al-Ramlī," whose adherents are known to this day as the "Ramliyya"; they are the Malikites.
§19 — Mīshawayh al-ʿUkbarī

After "Ismaʿīl," in the city of ʿUkbarā, there was "Mīshawayh al-ʿUkbarī," who was very weak in reflection and was, moreover, like one deranged according to what is reported of him — we shall mention this below. His adherents in ʿUkbarā are to this day called the "Mīshawiyya," and there has never been seen among them a scholar or a man of reflection.
§20 — Daniel al-Dāmaghānī (al-Qūmisī)
The last who held a doctrine, wrote books, and was followed by men was "Daniel al-Dāmaghānī," known as al-Qūmisī, whose description we have already given in the First Bab.
§21 — Summary, and the Karaites of the present age

These are the well-known, famous sects, so far as has reached us. As for the Karaites of this age, who issue from the doctrines we have mentioned, you will scarcely find two of them agreeing on everything: rather, this one dissents from that in one matter, and that one dissents from this in several. We shall later mention something of this. Let us now begin to set out what each sect held as its own.
: Arabic baʿda istiwāʾ al-mulk, "after the kingship was firmly established" — i.e. after the reigns of Saul and David consolidated the monarchy. Cf. Nemoy, HUCA 7 (1930), p. 321.

: The Cairo text reads mijlā/mujlā dhahab ("[image of] gold") here, but al-ʿijlayn ("the two calves") in the parallel just below; the citations that follow (1 Kgs 12) make clear the reference is to Jeroboam's two golden calves. Cf. Nemoy, HUCA 7, p. 321 n. 8.
: qawm min aṣḥābinā, "a group of our companions," i.e. earlier Karaite scholars (unnamed). The reading of Jeroboam's calves as substitutes for the Cherubim recurs among the early Karaites.

: al-tashbīh wa-l-tamthīl bi-l-muftaraḍ, "imitation and counterfeit of what was prescribed": Jeroboam designed his cult at Bethel and Dan as a deliberate replica of the Jerusalem Temple — priests for Levites, festival for festival, calf for Cherubim. This is Q's key argument that Jeroboam dissented in the place and form of worship, not in the object of worship.

: The rationalist–scriptural core of the bab: had Jeroboam been an idolater, he would have abolished the rites, not replaced them. The very act of substitution proves his intent was religious (though wrongheaded).
: The second citation ("in another place") repeats the first; Nemoy notes there is no such distinct verse, so Q is citing loosely from memory.
: Reading "וּבְחֻקֹּתֵיהֶם לֹא תֵלֵכוּ" (Lev 18:3) as a prohibition of the forbidden sexual unions that follow in the chapter, not of idolatry — the same exegesis given by Saadia.
: al-mawḍiʿ al-mukhtār, "the chosen place," rendering the biblical "the place that the LORD will choose" (Deut 12:5); Q uses it throughout as a cipher for the Jerusalem Temple.

: A reductio: read literally, "These are your gods who brought you up from Egypt" would have a not-yet-made calf accomplish the past Exodus — nonsense fit only for one "deprived of reason." Hence a non-literal reading is required.

: Q adopts the interpretation — already in Philo and the Midrash — that the calf represented one of the angelic faces (the ox-face of the cherubic vision), reducing the sin of the calf to an aesthetic-representational error rather than apostasy.
: yatawārathū, "inherited one from another": Jeroboam's successors received his doctrines as a transmitted tradition of leadership.
: A composite of the recurring refrain in Kings (1 Kgs 15:34; 16:19; 22:53, etc.), not a single verse.

: A characteristic methodological aside: Q justifies the length of the Jeroboam treatment — though the bab is meant only to name the sects — because the Jeroboam episode is the foundational interpretation of all subsequent Jewish schism.
: Arabic al-Kūtiyyīn, the Talmudic designation of the Samaritans, after the biblical account (2 Kgs 17:24) deriving them from Kutha in Mesopotamia.
: Sanballat the Horonite, leader of the Samaritans in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 2–4).

: Q here adopts the Rabbanite tradition of the "Men of the Great Assembly" (cf. Avot 1) in order to build his indictment: "Simeon the Just" is, on Q's reading, a late product of the Jeroboamite tradition, not the cornerstone of a genuine one.

: Rabban Gamaliel and the sanctification of the month by sighting of the new moon (M. Rosh ha-Shanah 2:8–9): Q cites it as evidence that the Rabbanites themselves admit deviation, exchanging fixed reckonings for internal rulings.

: The well-known Talmudic story of "the Oven of Akhnai" (B. Bava Metsiʿa 59b): even after divine signs and the heavenly voice (bat qol), the Rabbanites decreed against Eliezer and banished him — for Q, proof of their bad faith.
: The Sadducee/Karaite prohibition of marrying the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, established by analogy (qiyās) to the paternal aunt and the daughter-in-law forbidden in Lev 18.
: The Karaite reckoning of the Festival of Weeks from "the morrow of the Sabbath" (Lev 23:15) — i.e. the Sunday after Passover — against the Rabbanite reckoning from the second day of Passover.
: Arabic al-Maghāriyya, "the people of the caves." Modern scholarship has variously linked them to the Qumran sect or a kindred current; see Erder, Mourners of Zion, ch. 2.
: al-Iskandarānī, "the Alexandrian." Wolfson (1960) proposed identifying him with Philo of Alexandria, on the strength of Q's descriptions below.
: The book's name is uncertain in the manuscript (here transcribed in Hebrew letters); the reading and identification remain unsettled.
: An allusion to the ben Pandera traditions about Jesus in the Talmud and the Toledot Yeshu literature.
: Q develops his treatment of Christianity more fully in Maqala III (babs 17–18) and Maqala IV; an English translation of that material is in Nemoy, HUCA 7 (1930), pp. 363–397.
: Arabic ālāt al-qarʿ, "vessels of gourd." A small and poorly attested sect, traditionally located in Upper Egypt.
: al-Shām: medieval Syria–Palestine. The contrast is between the Babylonian academies (Sura, Pumbedita) and the academy of the Land of Israel.
: Arabic thalātha (the manuscript reading is uncertain; Nemoy/the editor differ); the precise referent — perhaps a tractate or a set of three disputed matters — is not certain.

: ʿObadiah / Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī / "al-Rāʿī," to whom Q devotes a full bab (11) below. See Erder, Mourners; Wasserstrom, Between Muslim and Jew (1995); Erder, "The Doctrine of Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī," JSAI 20 (1996).
: The Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān (r. 685–705), placing Abū ʿĪsā at the end of the 7th c.
: A community of ʿĪsawiyya at Damascus in the tenth century — a notable and singular notice.
: Treated more fully in bab 13 below. "Raʿyā" reflects the Aramaic for "shepherd," the title his sect gave its leader.

: The Abbasid caliph Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr (r. 754–775). ʿAnan b. David, the first Exilarch [of the movement], was active at Baghdad in the mid-8th c.; see Ben-Shammai, "Between Ananites and Karaites."

: Ḥazzānat Yannai, "the [liturgical] collection of Yannai," the great early payyetan (6th c.). The notice that Hai Gaon and his father (Sherira) translated ʿAnan's book from Aramaic into Hebrew is a striking Geonic-Karaite report.
: The traditional legend of ʿAnan's escape from death under al-Manṣūr; see Gil, A History of Palestine, s.v. ʿAnan.
: al-ʿUkbarī, from ʿUkbarā, a town on the Tigris between Baghdad and Sāmarrāʾ. Q devotes bab 15 to him below.
: The Abbasid caliph al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh (r. 833–842), placing Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī in the mid-9th c.
: Elijah's epitaph (2 Kgs 2:12), which Ismaʿīl is said to have claimed for himself — at once his self-conceit and the occasion of Q's mockery. Cf. Nemoy, Karaite Anthology (1952), pp. 50–53.
: Treated more fully in bab 14 below. Benjamin al-Nahāwandī is the chief Karaite authority before Q, whose doctrine of the "created angel" Q later criticizes sharply.
: al-qiyās, legal analogy. Benjamin, unlike ʿAnan, was reluctant to use open analogy and preferred to read Scripture by its explicit sense (al-naṣṣ).
: qiyās bi-muqaddimatayn wa-natīja, a syllogism of two premises and a conclusion: Benjamin admits this restricted (categorical-syllogistic) inference but not open analogical reasoning.
: Tiflīs (Tbilisi) in Georgia. Q notes that Mūsā al-Zaʿfarānī ("Abū ʿImrān al-Tiflīsī") settled there and won a following that persisted to Q's day.
: Ramla in Palestine; treated briefly in bab 16 below. The sect is poorly attested.
: Mīshawayh al-ʿUkbarī; a fuller notice follows in bab 17. See Erder, Mourners, ch. 3, the most extensive treatment in the scholarship.
: al-Dāmaghānī, from Dāmaghān in Persia. Daniel al-Qūmisī (of Qūmis, Persia), the leading Karaite of the Jerusalem "Mourners of Zion"; cf. bab 1, §3 above.
: A bridge-passage to babs 3–19: from here Q proceeds sect by sect, setting out the doctrines distinctive to each.
